common_name: Aunt Eily Crocosmia (Tall Bronze-Leaved Giant Montbretia Species)

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; this South African species is one of the tallest crocosmias grown, with strongly pleated bronze-green foliage and wiry black-purple flowering stems.

directions: Divide corm chains or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Aunt Eily is a robust South African species crocosmia, among the tallest grown in gardens, with broad, strongly pleated, upright bronze-green leaves and branched, dark, wiry stems that hold widely flared, orange-red flowers marked with darker red-brown spotting in the throat during mid to late summer. It is one of the more distinctly architectural crocosmia species, holding its blooms well above the foliage on stiff, near-black stems that read almost as a separate ornamental feature even before flowering. It multiplies steadily by corm offsets and benefits from division every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering. Site it toward the back of a border or among later-season perennials, since its height and bold pleated foliage can overwhelm smaller neighbors.

common_name: Potts's Crocosmia (Wild Parent Species of Montbretia)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Potts's crocosmia is, along with C. aurea, one of the two wild parent species of the popular hybrid Montbretia (C. x crocosmiiflora).

directions: Plant corms in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Potts's crocosmia is a more slender, narrower-leaved South African species than its cross-partner C. aurea, bearing slimmer arching stems of smaller, orange-red, funnel-shaped flowers in late summer above narrow, grassy, sword-like leaves. It was crossed with C. aurea in the late 1870s to produce the immensely popular hybrid Montbretia that now dominates garden crocosmia plantings, and the species itself is grown mainly by collectors and gardeners interested in crocosmia origins. It spreads by chains of linked corms and tolerates somewhat boggier soil than most crocosmia species, reflecting its native streamside and marsh-edge habitat. In colder zones treat it as it would be treated for tender montbretia relatives, lifting corms or applying a heavy winter mulch where marginally hardy.

common_name: Album Colchicum (Pure White Giant Autumn Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms 4-6 inches deep in late summer to early fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Album is a pure white, Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit selection of showy autumn crocus, among the finest white fall-blooming bulbs available.

directions: Set corms 4-6 inches deep and about 6-9 inches apart in a sunny to lightly shaded bed with rich, well-drained soil, planting in late summer so the large, goblet-shaped, pure-white flowers rise leafless from bare ground in early autumn. Album is widely regarded by bulb specialists as one of the very best white autumn-flowering bulbs, its substantial, pristine blooms standing out cleanly against dark mulch or evergreen groundcover rather than disappearing the way many white flowers do in bright light. Broad, glossy, strap-like leaves emerge the following spring, photosynthesize to recharge the corm, then die back and must be left to yellow naturally before removal. All parts are toxic if ingested, so site it away from grazing animals and small children, and mark plantings since the naked fall flowers can be startling to encounter unexpectedly.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Cilician colchicum is a free-flowering Turkish species that produces an unusually large number of star-shaped rosy-lilac blooms per corm.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in late summer, well before the leafless flowers appear. Native to the mountains of southern Turkey and named for the ancient region of Cilicia, this species is exceptionally floriferous, with each mature corm capable of producing a dozen or more star-shaped, rosy-lilac flowers in succession over several weeks in early to mid autumn, rather than the smaller handful typical of many colchicum species. The lance-shaped spring foliage is noticeably narrower and less bulky than that of C. byzantinum or C. speciosum, making it easier to tuck among later-emerging perennials that will mask the dying leaves. It naturalizes readily in sunny rock gardens, gravel beds, and turf. All plant parts are toxic if ingested and should be sited away from grazing animals or edible garden beds.

common_name: Autumn Queen Colchicum (Checkered Purple Autumn Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in late summer in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Autumn Queen bears large, strongly tessellated (checkered) reddish-purple flowers with a paler throat, opening leafless in early fall.

directions: Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in late summer, so the naked flowers can push through bare soil in early fall. Autumn Queen is a long-cultivated hybrid selection prized for its large, goblet-shaped flowers with a pronounced checkerboard (tessellated) pattern of deep reddish-purple over a paler pinkish-lilac ground, a more strongly marked pattern than is typical of most garden colchicum hybrids. The broad, glossy, strap-like leaves that follow the next spring must be left to die back naturally to recharge the corm before disappearing by early summer. It increases steadily by cormlets and is best left undisturbed for several years to build into a substantial flowering clump. All plant parts are toxic if ingested, so site it away from grazing animals and small children.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in late summer to very early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; unlike most snowdrops, Queen Olga's snowdrop flowers in autumn, typically before or just as its narrow leaves emerge.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in late summer to very early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to light shade, ideally in a warm, sheltered spot such as beneath deciduous shrubs or at a woodland edge. Named for Queen Olga of Greece, this species is one of the very few snowdrops that flowers in autumn rather than winter or spring, sending up small, nodding, honey-scented white flowers with green-marked inner petals from September into November, typically appearing before or just alongside its narrow, grass-like leaves rather than the leaves-first pattern of most other snowdrops. It is somewhat less cold-hardy and more particular about drainage and summer baking than the common G. nivalis, appreciating a drier summer dormancy period reflecting its native Greek, Sicilian, and Balkan mountain habitats. Once established it slowly forms a modest clump; divide and replant while still in leaf shortly after flowering for best results, and purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Wendy's Gold is a prized yellow-marked snowdrop cultivar, with a golden-yellow ovary and inner petal mark in place of the usual green.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally beneath deciduous trees where they receive good light before the canopy leafs out. Wendy's Gold, discovered in a Norfolk, England garden and named for the finder's wife, was one of the first widely distributed yellow snowdrop cultivars and remains among the most vigorous, with a bright golden-yellow ovary and inner petal marking replacing the green found in the common snowdrop, set off by rounded, pure-white outer petals on a plant of good height and increase for a yellow form. It flowers in late winter, among the earlier bulbs of the season. Yellow snowdrops are generally slower to establish and less vigorous than green-marked forms, so give it a settled, undisturbed spot with reliably moist but well-drained soil; divide and transplant clumps only while still in leaf ('in the green'), immediately after flowering, for the best transplant success. Never dig from the wild; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba is a pure white-flowered selection of glory-of-the-snow, a clean-colored companion for the typical blue species and pink cultivars.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; glory-of-the-snow naturalizes readily under deciduous trees and in lawns. Alba bears the same star-shaped flowers and early-spring bloom time as the typical blue species, but in clean, pure white with no blue tinge, opening among the earliest bulbs of the year and often overlapping with the last snowdrops and crocus. Its white flowers combine well with blue-flowered glory-of-the-snow, 'Pink Giant', and other very early bulbs for a mixed drift, and read cleanly in shadier spots where blue flowers can look muddy in low light. Allow the grass-like foliage to die back naturally after flowering before mowing over naturalized plantings; it self-seeds and multiplies by offset bulbs to form larger colonies over time.
